28bc72c9.title: Pregnancy questions, answered
28bc72c9.subtitle: Answers to common questions from your OB/GYN team at Women's Specialists of Clear Lake

subsections.title: When should I schedule my first visit?
subsections.body: Schedule as soon as pregnancy is confirmed — ideally between 8–10 weeks. We'll confirm the pregnancy, estimated due date, and start your care plan.

subsections.title: How often will I be seen?
subsections.body: Monthly until 28 weeks · every 2 weeks 28–36 weeks · weekly 36–40 weeks · twice weekly after 40 weeks.

subsections.title: What prenatal vitamins should I take?
subsections.body: Begin a prenatal vitamin with at least 400–800 mcg of folic acid as soon as possible. Start before conception if planning a pregnancy.

subsections.title: How much extra should I eat?
subsections.body: Extra calorie needs: 0 extra in 1st trimester · ~340/day 2nd · ~450/day 3rd trimester. Focus on nutrient quality, not just quantity.

subsections.title: What medications are safe?
subsections.body: Generally safe: Tylenol (acetaminophen), Tums, Zofran (with approval), prenatal vitamins. Avoid NSAIDs (ibuprofen, Advil) especially after 20 weeks.

subsections.title: Can I exercise?
subsections.body: Yes! 30 minutes of moderate exercise most days is recommended unless complications arise. Walking, swimming, and prenatal yoga are excellent choices.

subsections.title: Can I travel?
subsections.body: Generally safe until 36 weeks. Avoid long trips after 28 weeks without medical clearance. Stay hydrated and move frequently on long trips.

subsections.title: 8–10 weeks
subsections.body: Confirm pregnancy, EDD, baseline labs, genetic counseling

subsections.title: 11–14 weeks
subsections.body: First trimester screen, NT ultrasound, NIPT if desired

subsections.title: 16–18 weeks
subsections.body: Quad screen, hear heartbeat, discuss anatomy scan

subsections.title: 18–22 weeks
subsections.body: Anatomy ultrasound — detailed fetal survey

subsections.title: 24–28 weeks
subsections.body: Gestational diabetes screen (1-hr glucose), Tdap

subsections.title: 28–36 weeks
subsections.body: Every 2 weeks; RhoGAM if Rh-negative

subsections.title: 36–40 weeks
subsections.body: Weekly; GBS swab; birth plan discussion

subsections.title: 40+ weeks
subsections.body: Twice weekly; NST; discuss induction options

subsections.title: Call us immediately / Go to L&D
items: Signs of preeclampsia: severe headache, vision changes, swelling in face/hands

subsections.title: After-hours emergency
subsections.body: Call our office or go directly to Clear Lake Regional Medical Center L&D

subsections.title: Recommended & safe
items: Flu vaccine: Every flu season (any trimester)
COVID-19: Recommended; discuss with Dr. Klein

subsections.title: Avoid live vaccines in pregnancy
subsections.body: MMR, Varicella, Live flu mist, Yellow fever

subsections.title: Protecting you and your newborn
subsections.body: Vaccines are the safest way to protect you and your newborn from serious illness.

sections.title: Questions? We're here for you 24/7
sections.body: No question is too small. Call our office at (281) 557-0300 during office hours. For after-hours emergencies, leave a message and our on-call provider will return your call. We're honored to be part of your pregnancy journey.

7d319ac9.title: When to call your doctor
7d319ac9.subtitle: A patient guide
7d319ac9.intro: Congratulations on your pregnancy. Most symptoms in pregnancy are normal and related to hormonal and physical changes. However, some symptoms can be warning signs of a serious condition. Please contact our office or seek urgent care immediately if you experience any of the following:

sections.title: Call 911 or go to the ER immediately
items: Shortness of breath at rest or difficulty breathing
Thoughts of harming yourself or others
Heavy vaginal bleeding (soaking 1 pad/hour or large clots)

subsections.title: Bleeding or fluid concerns
items: Gush or steady leakage of fluid from the vagina

subsections.title: Pain
items: Severe cramping not relieved by rest
Persistent right upper abdominal pain (under ribs)
Severe back pain with pelvic pressure

subsections.title: Headache or vision changes
items: Severe headache not improved with rest or Tylenol
Blurred vision, flashing lights, or temporary vision loss
Sudden swelling of face, hands, or around eyes

subsections.title: Blood pressure / Preeclampsia symptoms
items: Feeling generally unwell in second half of pregnancy

subsections.title: Fever or infection
items: Persistent cough with shortness of breath

subsections.title: Decreased baby movement (after 28 weeks)
subsections.body: Movement should not decrease toward the end of pregnancy.
items: Noticeable decrease in baby’s usual movement pattern
Fewer than 10 movements in 2 hours during active time

sections.title: Mental health matters
items: Trouble sleeping unrelated to pregnancy discomfort
Feeling overwhelmed or unable to cope

sections.title: Common symptoms that are usually normal
sections.body: Still call if severe or concerning to you.
items: Mild shortness of breath with activity
Braxton Hicks contractions (irregular, not painful, resolve with rest)

sections.title: Trust your instincts
sections.body: If something feels wrong, call. You know your body best. If you are unsure whether a symptom is serious, it is always appropriate to contact our office for guidance.

sections.title: Contact & after hours
sections.body:
Office Phone: 281-557-0300 | After Hours: Follow the answering service instructions to reach the on-call physician.

Questions? Contact our office. This handout is for educational purposes only and does not replace personalized medical advice from your provider.

7d319ac9.clinicalUpdates: Dr. Klein updated the decreased-movement threshold to 28 weeks on September 7, 2026. The original PDF retains its earlier wording.

14a92cf3.title: Vaccines & pregnancy
14a92cf3.subtitle: Protecting you and your baby — before, during, and after pregnancy
14a92cf3.intro: When you get vaccinated, you aren't just protecting yourself — your body makes antibodies that cross the placenta and give your baby early protection during the first months of life, before they are old enough for their own vaccines. Some vaccines are best given before pregnancy, three are recommended during every pregnancy, and a few are given after delivery to catch up.
14a92cf3.copyright: © 2026 Women's Specialists of Clear Lake · Patient Education Material

subsections.title: The best time to get fully protected is before you conceive
items: We check your immunity to measles, rubella & chickenpox (varicella)
MMR and varicella are live vaccines — get them, then wait 4 weeks before trying to conceive
Flu shot any time you may become pregnant
Catch up on HPV vaccine through age 26
Hepatitis A & B and pneumococcal if you have risk factors
A preconception visit is the ideal time to review your vaccine history

sections.title: During pregnancy — three vaccines, every pregnancy

subsections.title: Tdap · 27–36 weeks · Every pregnancy
subsections.body: Protects against tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis (whooping cough). Whooping cough is especially dangerous for newborns — it can cause them to stop breathing and turn blue. Getting Tdap in the third trimester lets your antibodies cross the placenta and protect your baby from birth until their own vaccine at 2 months.

subsections.title: Flu (Influenza) · Any trimester · Flu season
subsections.body: Pregnancy changes your immune, heart, and lung function, making you much more likely to become seriously ill from the flu. The flu also raises the risk of premature labor. The shot passes antibodies to your baby, protecting them before their own vaccine at 6 months.
items: Get it by end of October if possible
Flu shot only — not the nasal spray

subsections.title: RSV (Abrysvo) · 32–36 weeks · Sept–Jan
subsections.body: RSV is the leading cause of infant hospitalization in the U.S. The Pfizer vaccine (Abrysvo) is the only RSV vaccine approved in pregnancy. Antibodies pass to your baby and protect against severe RSV for their first 6 months. If you don't get the RSV vaccine, your baby can instead receive an antibody shot (nirsevimab) after birth.

subsections.title: 1st trimester
subsections.body: Flu shot if season is active

subsections.title: 2nd trimester
subsections.body: Flu shot if season is active

subsections.title: 3rd trimester · 27–36 weeks
subsections.body: Tdap every pregnancy

subsections.title: 3rd trimester · 32–36 weeks
subsections.body: RSV (Abrysvo) Sept–Jan only

subsections.title: Flu season (any trimester)
subsections.body: Flu shot by end of October

subsections.title: Catch up on anything you couldn't get during pregnancy
items: If you were non-immune to measles, rubella, or chickenpox, get those vaccines now
These live vaccines are safe while breastfeeding
Start or finish the HPV series if you're age 26 or younger
Catch up on any Hepatitis A/B or pneumococcal doses you still need

sections.title: Vaccines to avoid during pregnancy
items: Live vaccines are not given while pregnant: MMR, varicella (chickenpox), and the nasal-spray flu (FluMist) — get these before or after pregnancy
It's perfectly fine for your family members to receive these live vaccines
If a live vaccine is given before a pregnancy is known, don't worry — no fetal harm has ever been reported

sections.title: Are these vaccines safe?
sections.body: Yes. The flu shot, Tdap, and RSV vaccine are studied extensively in pregnancy and recommended by ACOG, the CDC, and the AAP. The vaccines given during pregnancy are not live and cannot give you the disease. Side effects are mild and temporary — arm soreness, low-grade fever, or fatigue for 1–2 days — signs your immune system is responding. Vaccines do not cause autism or infertility.

sections.title: Questions about vaccines?
sections.body: Talk to us at your next visit. We're happy to review your vaccination history and make sure you and your baby are fully protected — before, during, and after pregnancy. No question is too small. You can also find reliable information at cdc.gov/vaccines.
